articles.title: Central Park adapts to climate change while helping New York stay cool
articles.summary: In the heart of Manhattan in New York City, the effects of climate change are becoming increasingly visible.
articles.content:
New York’s Central Park – one of the world’s most recognisable landmarks – is experiencing heavier downpours, flooding and soil erosion, while prolonged heatwaves are putting pressure on the ecosystem as well as visitors.

But the park also helps New York cope with the heat. It helps cool the city, clean the air, capture stormwater and gives people a place to escape the heat under the trees. The temperature in the park can be around 5°Celsius (10°F) lower than on surrounding streets, according to the Central Park Climate Lab.

UN News/Evgeniya Kleshcheva

“Central Park and urban parks are so much more than just recreation spaces,” said Yanina Kupava, a Director at the Central Park Conservancy. “They are vital urban green infrastructure.”

UN News visited Central Park on a hot summer day, just weeks before world leaders gather at UN Headquarters for the General Assembly’s General Debate.

As politicians and experts discuss how cities can adapt to a warming planet, some of those solutions can already be seen just a few blocks away in the park.

Plants for a new climate

If the main challenge in the 1980s was restoring the park – which had suffered from years of neglect after the 1970s fiscal crisis – today the priority is to preserve its historic landscape in the face of a changing climate.

The Park’s celebrated crabapple alleys, for example, have become one of its most spectacular sights in spring, when branches burst into white, pink and purple blossom. Park staff say the setting is so romantic that the number of marriage proposals there is “wild”.

But winters that are too warm could prevent apple trees from flowering altogether, while spells of warm weather in February can cause magnolias and cherry trees to bloom too soon.

UN News/Evgeniya Kleshcheva

“If they bloom too early then a late frost can really impact the trees,” Ms. Kupava explained. “And if we get milder and milder winters those trees might have trouble blooming and pollinating.”

Being located in the middle of a major metropolis places additional pressure on the park’s plants and wildlife. New York, like other densely built-up urban areas, heats up faster and retains heat longer than surrounding suburban and rural areas.

The Central Park Conservancy, the body in charge of maintaining the park, is thus looking for plant varieties that may be better adapted to the new climate and is experimenting with plants from different climate zones.

The challenge is a delicate one: adapting a landscape conceived in the 19th Century to 21st-Century conditions without allowing Central Park to lose the character that has made it recognisable around the world.

'Not a leaf goes to waste'

At a working site in the northern part of the park, piles of leaves, weeds and other plant material – including food waste from staff facilities – are now being turned into compost.

It is used to give plants the strength to cope with changing climatic conditions. It is also used to enrich garden soil, help restore heavily used lawns and to reduce surface runoff during heavy rain.

“We want all of that wonderful material to stay in the park for those nutrients to get returned back to the soil,” Ms. Kupava said.

The Conservancy now plans to expand the site so that even more material can be processed – keeping as much as possible out of landfill.

Saving every drop

Water conservation is another priority.

New underground infrastructure will allow water to circulate between the water bodies in the northern section of Central Park, halting the need to continually draw potable water into the system.

“It’s not going to be something that is highly visible to the public, but the water savings to the city will be immense,” Ms. Kupava said.

At the same time, the Conservancy is gradually replacing petrol- and diesel-powered machinery with electric alternatives, from smaller power tools to larger mowers, tractors and even trash compactors. Functioning equipment is not simply discarded, but electric alternatives are considered as machinery needs to be replaced and suitable technologies become available.

A lesson for cities everywhere

Although the Conservancy’s work is centred on one park, its story offers lessons far beyond New York.

UN News/Evgeniya Kleshcheva

More than half of the world’s population already lives in cities, and by 2050 that figure is expected to approach 70 per cent. As temperatures rise and flood risks increase, urban green spaces are becoming ever more important.

“I think what other cities can take away is that long-term investment in their green infrastructure is critical. It really helps cities have a better environment in the day-to-day but also helps them be prepared for future climate and environmental change,” said Ms. Kupava.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article describes how Central Park is adapting to climate change by implementing sustainable practices that help cool New York City, conserve water, reduce waste, and preserve biodiversity. These efforts have broad significance as they provide a model for urban green infrastructure that benefits millions of city dwellers and addresses climate resilience on a large scale.
articles.personality_title: Central Park adapts to climate change to keep New York cooler and greener

**Context** – Central Park, a famous park in the middle of New York City, is facing challenges from climate change. The city is experiencing heavier rain, flooding, and longer heatwaves, which affect both the park’s plants and the people who visit.

They are choosing new types of plants that can live better in warmer weather, turning leaves and plant waste into compost to feed the soil, and saving water by improving underground systems. They are also switching from gas-powered machines to electric ones to reduce pollution.

**Impact** – These efforts help keep the park cooler—about 5 degrees Celsius cooler than nearby streets—which makes the city more comfortable during hot days. The park also cleans the air, captures rainwater, and gives people a cool place to rest. This work shows how important parks are for city life, not just for fun but for health and safety as the climate changes.

**What's next step** – The Conservancy plans to expand composting and continue finding plants that can survive the changing weather. They will also keep replacing old machines with electric ones. These steps will help the park stay healthy and continue to protect the city from heat and storms.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Central Park is changing how it grows plants, saves water, and reduces waste to help New York City stay cooler and greener as the climate changes.

articles.personality_title_es: Central Park se adapta al cambio climático para mantener Nueva York más fresca y verde
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Central Park, un parque famoso en el centro de Nueva York, enfrenta desafíos por el cambio climático. La ciudad tiene lluvias más fuertes, inundaciones y olas de calor más largas, lo que afecta a las plantas del parque y a las personas que lo visitan.

**Qué pasó** – Para enfrentar estos problemas, el grupo que cuida Central Park, llamado Central Park Conservancy, está haciendo cambios. También están cambiando máquinas que usan gasolina por máquinas eléctricas para reducir la contaminación.

El parque también limpia el aire, captura el agua de lluvia y ofrece un lugar fresco para descansar. Esto muestra lo importante que son los parques en la ciudad, no solo para divertirse, sino para la salud y la seguridad ante el cambio climático.

**Próximo paso** – La Conservancy planea ampliar el compostaje y seguir buscando plantas que puedan sobrevivir al clima cambiante. También continuará reemplazando maquinaria antigua por eléctrica. Estos pasos ayudarán a que el parque se mantenga saludable y siga protegiendo la ciudad del calor y las tormentas.

**Resumen en una frase** – Central Park está cambiando cómo cultiva plantas, ahorra agua y reduce desechos para ayudar a que Nueva York se mantenga más fresca y verde frente al cambio climático.

articles.title: As wildfires spread north, UN agencies race to help Europe adapt
articles.summary: As the climate warms, the threat of wildfires is spreading in Europe. How can historically cooler and wetter countries prepare?
articles.content:
Human activity causes most of the wildfires breaking out across Europe, but their spread, speed and intensity are strongly affected by the warmer, drier conditions associated with climate change as well as with changing land use.

More than 600,000 hectares of land have burned within European Union countries in the first eight months of 2026, according to the European Forest Fire Information System.

That’s below the area recorded by the same date in 2025 (the worst year on record), but it far exceeds the 20-year average of around 280,000 hectares, and preparing for wildfires is key, UN agencies say.

Risks are growing

While most fires have occured in historically fire-prone countries such as France and Spain, extremely dry conditions are putting many areas in Western and Central Europe, including the UK and southern Scandinavia, at increased risk.

In the immediate future, wildfire risks may be compounded by the developing El Niño, a recurrent natural climate phenomenon, which can further influence temperatures and rainfall patterns and increase the likelihood of climate extremes.

Many countries with a history of wildfires are now experiencing more frequent and larger blazes, over longer periods. At the same time, other countries in traditionally cooler or wetter areas are also preparing for the prospect of dealing with more wildfires.

Scotland’s burning forests

A wildfire took hold in the Cairngorms mountains of Scotland in mid-July. The area has experienced wildfires before, but due to this year’s exceptionally dry conditions, the fire penetrated the dry peat layer, causing hotspots and flare-ups that resisted containment.

More than 500 firefighters fought the blazes, with aerial support to put out fires – while bulldozers were called in to dig firebreaks.

High winds pushed the unpredictable blaze towards the village of Nethy Bridge.

Evacuation orders

Nine days on from the outbreak, Police Scotland declared a major incident and many of Nethy Bridge’s 600 residents were evacuated, including James MacEwan, who described a worrying stretch of days without any rainfall amid the growing blaze.

“We were very fortunate that the wind remained from the west and took the fire towards the hills, otherwise we would have had a serious threat to property and possibly life,” he said. “The downside was that this took the fire into relatively inaccessible terrain and made containing it extremely difficult.”

It was over a month from the time that the fire started until the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service officially stood down firefighting crews.

© Climate Visuals/Alastair

Preparing for the future

The risk is now extending far beyond the Mediterranean, said Will Hayes, a researcher with the UK’s Leverhulme Centre for Wildfires, Environment and Society.

Growing wildfire concerns have already emerged in the Atlantic uplands of Ireland and Scotland as well as other parts of Northern and Central Europe, he said.

“These areas are not becoming Mediterranean landscapes, but traditionally wetter, cooler regions are now experiencing more frequent windows where increasing amounts of vegetation is dry enough to burn and fires can spread,” Mr. Hayes warned.

“People should not assume that wet or green landscapes are immune to fire. During dry, warm and windy periods, vegetation can become highly flammable, even in upland and northern regions.”

He suggested avoiding campfires, barbecues and careless ignition sources – such as cigarette lighters – during high-risk weather, and following local fire warnings.

Assessing risks

Preparedness for wildfires is also important at the national level, Mr. Hayes said.

“Wildfire prevention is not just about fire services, it is about how landscapes are managed before they burn,” he explained. “Wildfire risk should be treated as a land-use, climate-adaptation and public-health issue, not just an emergency-response problem.”

The World Health Organization (WHO) Strategic Toolkit for Assessing Risks (STAR) methodology enables public health authorities to work alongside other sectors to rapidly conduct a strategic and evidence-based assessment of public health risks that includes the risk of heat and wildfires.

Smarter readiness

Countries such as Cyprus and Ireland have recently completed their first-ever assessment workshops, which used the STAR methodology to identify and prioritise pressing health hazards, from heatwaves to wildfires.

The workshops lay the groundwork for smarter, more strategic emergency preparedness and readiness investments.

WHO has run 38 national strategic risk assessment workshops in Europe since 2018, and its STAR is recognised as one of the core elements of international health regulations (IHR) and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction.

Growing public health threat

Tanja Schmidt, WHO Europe’s programme manager on preparedness in the health security division, said extreme heat and wildfires are no longer only environmental emergencies.

“They are growing public health threats that directly affect people’s health as well as health systems,” she said.

“Across the region, countries are increasingly using all-hazards national risk assessments to understand climate-driven risks, identify cascading impacts and prioritise preparedness actions. Ultimately, this helps protect communities, prioritising those most vulnerable and ensuring that health systems are ready to respond.”

Learn more about WHO’s risk assessment tool kit here.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.personality_title: Europe strengthens wildfire preparedness as risks rise beyond the south
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Wildfires have long affected southern Europe, but rising temperatures and drier weather linked to climate change are now increasing fire risks in northern and western parts of the continent, including places like Scotland and the UK.

**What happened** – In 2026, over 600,000 hectares have burned in the European Union, more than double the 20-year average. Scotland faced a major wildfire in the Cairngorms mountains that lasted over a month and forced evacuations. In response, the United Nations and World Health Organization (WHO) are helping countries use new risk assessment methods to better prepare for wildfires and related health threats.

**Impact** – This situation is unique because it shows that even cooler and wetter regions, once considered safe from wildfires, now face serious fire risks. Countries are moving beyond emergency firefighting to focus on managing landscapes and public health strategies before fires start. The WHO’s Strategic Toolkit for Assessing Risks (STAR) helps governments identify dangers like heatwaves and wildfires early, improving readiness and protecting vulnerable communities.

**What's next step** – More countries in northern and central Europe are expected to use the STAR method and similar tools to plan for wildfires and heat risks. This means better coordination between firefighters, health officials, and land managers to reduce damage and keep people safe as climate conditions change.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Europe is expanding its wildfire preparation efforts to new regions by using strategic health and land management tools to face growing fire risks caused by climate change.

articles.personality_title_es: Europa refuerza la preparación contra incendios forestales ante el aumento del riesgo más allá del sur
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los incendios forestales han afectado durante mucho tiempo al sur de Europa, pero el aumento de las temperaturas y el clima más seco relacionados con el cambio climático están incrementando los riesgos de incendios en el norte y oeste del continente, incluyendo lugares como Escocia y el Reino Unido.

**Qué pasó** – En 2026, más de 600,000 hectáreas han ardido en la Unión Europea, más del doble del promedio de 20 años. Escocia enfrentó un gran incendio en las montañas Cairngorms que duró más de un mes y forzó evacuaciones. En respuesta, las Naciones Unidas y la Organización Mundial de la Salud (OMS) están ayudando a los países a usar nuevos métodos de evaluación de riesgos para prepararse mejor ante incendios y amenazas de salud relacionadas.

**Impacto** – Esta situación es única porque muestra que incluso regiones más frías y húmedas, antes consideradas seguras contra incendios, ahora enfrentan riesgos serios. Los países están pasando de solo apagar incendios a enfocarse en manejar el paisaje y la salud pública antes que ocurran los incendios. La Herramienta Estratégica para Evaluar Riesgos (STAR) de la OMS ayuda a los gobiernos a identificar temprano peligros como olas de calor e incendios, mejorando la preparación y protección de las comunidades vulnerables.

**Próximo paso** – Se espera que más países del norte y centro de Europa usen el método STAR y herramientas similares para planificar riesgos de incendios y calor. Esto significa mejor coordinación entre bomberos, funcionarios de salud y gestores de tierras para reducir daños y proteger a la gente ante el cambio climático.

**Una frase clave** – Europa amplía sus esfuerzos de preparación contra incendios a nuevas regiones usando herramientas estratégicas de salud y manejo de tierras para enfrentar el creciente riesgo por el cambio climático.

articles.title: Litter pick collects 50 bags of rubbish from river
articles.summary: A litter picking group gathers every month to remove rubbish from the River Wear in Durham.
articles.content:
A litter picking group which removes rubbish from a river collected more than 50 bags of rubbish at their latest gathering.

The Durham City Riverscape Community formed just before the coronavirus pandemic to carry out monthly litter picks along the River Wear.

The group estimated it had collected tonnes of waste from the water since the start, including a large fridge earlier this year.

Lead volunteer Graham Hollingwood said the group was approaching the 1,000 bag milestone which "just shows how much work goes into protecting our riverbanks" and the "phenomenal" efforts of volunteers.

He said pulling the full sized fridge freezer out of the river was their biggest challenge to date but the team proved equal to it.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a community-led environmental cleanup effort with significant tangible impact, removing large amounts of waste from a local river, which benefits the ecosystem and public spaces. The group's sustained monthly action, approaching 1,000 bags collected, demonstrates meaningful and ongoing positive environmental impact with clear substance and significance for the local community and environment.
articles.personality_title: Durham group collects 50 bags of rubbish from River Wear
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – A community group in Durham called the Durham City Riverscape Community started meeting just before the coronavirus pandemic. Their goal is to clean up rubbish along the River Wear every month.

**What happened** – In their latest cleanup, the group collected more than 50 bags of rubbish from the river area. Since they began, they have removed many tonnes of waste, including a large fridge freezer pulled out earlier this year.

**Impact** – The group is close to reaching 1,000 bags of rubbish collected, showing how much effort goes into keeping the riverbanks clean. Removing a full-sized fridge from the river was a big challenge, but the volunteers succeeded. Their work helps protect the local environment and makes the river area nicer for everyone.

**What's next step** – The group plans to continue their monthly cleanups and aims to keep removing rubbish from the river. Their ongoing effort will help keep the river cleaner and healthier over time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A dedicated Durham community group has removed nearly 1,000 bags of rubbish from the River Wear, improving the environment through regular cleanups.
